_about: V1.6 art/design layer: the DISCOVER card and one interaction for each new deepening card (CARD-07–CARD-14). Statements, reveals and KEEP THIS lines come from the V1.6 curriculum's deepening cards; interaction wording follows the V1.6 integration brief and the clarity rules (every screen asks a question, short options, no paragraphs). No new historical claims, no NOW hooks.

discovery_cards.title: WHO CONTROLS THE IMAGE?
discovery_cards.statement: Representation is power when images shape what people think is possible or true.
discovery_cards.reveal: Images do not simply reflect Black life; they can help define who appears human, dangerous, beautiful, respectable, modern, or worthy.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Richard J. Powell, Black Art and Culture in the 20th Century

discovery_cards.title: WHO IS BLACK ART FOR?
discovery_cards.statement: Audience changes what art is asked to do.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black artists have repeatedly argued over whether the work should persuade outsiders, serve Black communities, pursue artistic freedom, protest injustice, or do several things at once.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Richard J. Powell, Black Art and Culture in the 20th Century

discovery_cards.title: ART AS EVIDENCE
discovery_cards.statement: An image can document reality and still raise the question: who framed the story?
discovery_cards.reveal: A photograph or visual record can become evidence, memory, witness, and political leverage—but framing and circulation still shape what viewers understand.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Richard J. Powell, Black Art and Culture in the 20th Century

discovery_cards.title: THE ARTIST AS ORGANIZER
discovery_cards.statement: A movement can have a studio, a gallery, a magazine, or a design guild.
discovery_cards.reveal: Artists can organize not only through messages in their work but by building collectives, spaces, networks, and institutions that let cultural work survive and circulate.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Richard J. Powell + The Black Experience in Design

discovery_cards.title: SYSTEMS ARE DESIGNED TOO
discovery_cards.statement: If a system produces an outcome repeatedly, ask how it was designed.
discovery_cards.reveal: Schools, services, platforms, streets, forms, interfaces, and institutions all embody design choices about access, priorities, behavior, and outcomes.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — The Black Experience in Design — Eddie Opara and anthology framing

discovery_cards.title: DESIGN AS CARE
discovery_cards.statement: Care becomes structural when people can help shape the conditions they live inside.
discovery_cards.reveal: Design can redistribute access and decision-making by shaping spaces, processes, and institutions around the people most affected by them.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — The Black Experience in Design — community design / Infrastructure of Care

discovery_cards.title: WHO OWNS THE PLATFORM?
discovery_cards.statement: Visibility is not the same thing as control.
discovery_cards.reveal: A platform can give Black people visibility and voice while someone else still controls the rules, data, archive, reach, and economic value.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Black Futures + The Black Experience in Design

discovery_cards.title: WHO GETS TO IMAGINE THE FUTURE?
discovery_cards.statement: Before people build a different world, they have to imagine one.
discovery_cards.reveal: Imagining Black futures is a form of cultural power: before institutions, technologies, or communities can be built differently, people must be able to picture Black life continuing and flourishing differently.
discovery_cards.source: V1.6 art/design layer — Black Futures + The Black Experience in Design
